slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by positioning this section as the algebraic bridge after duality and saddle functions. Bifunctions are no longer just perturbation devices; they now behave like generalized arrows. The lecture will keep three questions visible: what operation is being performed, what dual operation it induces, and which regularity condition keeps the identity exact.

slides.title: Linear Model
slides.notes: Use the linear case to fix intuition before the notation gets heavier. A graph indicator says that all allowed pairs lie on the graph of a map. Its adjoint is the graph indicator of the transpose map, with the arrow reversed. Every later identity should look like this once specialized to matrices.

slides.title: Addition
slides.notes: Present addition as a resource split. The output x is decomposed into two pieces, one paid for by F1 and the other by F2, and the cheapest split defines the new bifunction. This is exactly why the dual value against x-star becomes a sum of two dual readings.

slides.title: Adjoint Of Addition
slides.notes: Slow down here because this is the first place where formal algebra meets regularity. The theorem is not just a symbolic rule. It says that infimal convolution and adjoint commute when the two parameter domains overlap in a robust relative-interior sense. If that robustness fails, closure is the repair mechanism.

slides.title: Scaling
slides.notes: Treat scaling as the easy control case. The graph function is moved by a one-to-one linear transformation, so convexity, closedness, and properness move with it. The dual equation is also clean: scaling the bifunction scales the inner-product reading and gives the same scalar action after taking the adjoint.

slides.title: Image Of A Function
slides.notes: This operation connects bifunction algebra with ordinary convex functions. Think of f as a cost assigned to the source space and F as a generalized transport rule. The image function asks for the cheapest source and transport certificate that reaches x. The adjoint formula is the dual version of that same routing problem.

slides.title: Composition
slides.notes: Define product as the operation that makes bifunctions act like arrows. F moves from the source space to a middle space, G moves from the middle space to the target, and the product minimizes over the hidden middle variable. In the linear case this is exactly matrix multiplication, with the order carefully preserved.

slides.title: Adjoint Of Composition
slides.notes: Make this the conceptual center of the lecture. Product moves forward through F and then G. The adjoint product moves backward through G-star and then F-star, which is written as F-star G-star because function composition is read from right to left. The small matrix residual in the notebook is the finite-dimensional audit of this rule.

slides.title: Domain Gate
slides.notes: Use this slide as a unifying diagnostic rather than a separate technical aside. Each theorem asks whether the spaces where the two objects can actually communicate overlap robustly. Relative interior is the language for robust overlap inside affine hulls, and it is what keeps infima, suprema, and adjoints from losing boundary information.

slides.title: Inner Product
slides.notes: Introduce the generalized inner product as the scalar that survives when a convex function and a concave function are paired through Fenchel duality. It is not automatically defined; the max-side and min-side expressions must agree. Once they do, conjugating both functions reverses the sign, which is exactly the behavior needed for adjoint transport.

slides.title: Transport Identity
slides.notes: This theorem is the payoff for defining the generalized inner product. It says that pairing after pushing a function forward through F gives the same scalar as pairing before the push, after pulling the dual object back through F-star. The sign changes in the other equalities come from conjugating convex and concave partners.

slides.title: Co-Finite Case
slides.notes: Co-finiteness is where the algebra begins to feel like ordinary linear algebra again. The domains are full, adjoints remain co-finite, and the main addition and product identities no longer carry the same boundary anxiety. This special case is useful because it tells students what the general theorems are trying to approximate.

slides.title: Numerical Lab
slides.notes: Tie the lecture back to the assigned notebook. The matrices are deliberately small so students can multiply them by hand or inspect the residual numerically. The point is not that matrices prove the full bifunction theorem. The point is that the finite model makes the order reversal and the pairing convention impossible to ignore.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as controlled hypothesis testing. Students should avoid changing the whole example at once. Changing order tests non-commutativity, changing the middle cost tests the product definition, and changing domains tests the relative-interior assumptions. Each experiment should end with a visible residual or closure diagnosis.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close with the checklist rather than another theorem. Each operation has a concrete construction, a dual or adjoint reading, and a regularity condition that determines whether closure is needed. The central memory hook is that composition moves forward through G after F, while the adjoint route moves backward through G-star and then F-star.
